function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

Here’s a quick rundown of the most common ways to get a fresh cake delivered to your door—plus a few extra tips so you can pick the best option for your needs:

| Option | What it offers | Typical price range | When it’s best |
|--------|----------------|---------------------|----------------|
| **Local bakeries** (e.g., Mom & Pop shops, artisanal bakeries) | Custom designs, seasonal flavors, often fresher ingredients | $20–$80+ per cake | When you want something unique, support a small business, or need a special design |
| **Big‑box grocery stores** (Walmart, Target, Kroger, Safeway, Publix, etc.) | Ready‑made cakes, sometimes custom orders, usually cheaper | $15–$50 | When you’re on a budget or need a quick pick‑up |
| **National chains** (Costco, Sam’s Club, Trader Joe’s, Whole Foods) | Bulk‑size cakes, limited flavor selection, sometimes “custom” options | $25–$70 | When you’re feeding a crowd or want a high‑quality store brand |
| **Online food‑delivery apps** (Uber Eats, DoorDash, Grubhub, Postmates, Instacart) | Same menu as the restaurant/bakery, plus delivery fee | $30–$100+ (incl. tip & fees) | When you want convenience, have a tight deadline, or want to compare multiple shops at once |
| **Specialty cake shops** (Cake Boss, Magnolia Bakery, Baked by Melissa, etc.) | Signature flavors, premium packaging, often nationwide shipping | $40–$120+ | When you want a brand‑name cake or a specific style (e.g., cupcakes, sheet cakes) |
| **E‑commerce sites** (Amazon Fresh, Thrive Market, Boxed) | Grocery‑style delivery, sometimes ready‑to‑eat cakes | $20–$60 | When you’re already shopping online and want everything in one box |
| **Custom cake designers** (local artists, wedding planners, event venues) | Fully customized designs, professional quality | $50–$200+ | When you need a show‑stopping centerpiece for a wedding, party, or corporate event |

### How to choose

1. **Know your deadline** – Most local bakeries can’t guarantee same‑day delivery unless you call ahead. Delivery apps usually list estimated arrival times.
2. **Check reviews** – Look at recent ratings on Google, Yelp, or the app itself. A cake that looks great in photos may taste different.
3. **Ask about ingredients** – If you have dietary restrictions (gluten‑free, vegan, nut allergies), confirm that the shop can accommodate them.
4. **Factor in delivery fees** – Apps charge a base fee plus a tip; local shops may offer free pickup or a flat delivery rate.
5. **Consider the occasion** – For a simple birthday, a store‑brand cake might suffice. For a wedding or milestone, a custom design from a specialty shop can make a bigger impact.

### Quick start guide

1. **Call your favorite local bakery** – Ask if they deliver or if you can place an order online. Many now accept orders through their own website or via a simple phone call.
2. **Use a delivery app** – Search “cake” or “bakery” in the app, filter by rating, and see real‑time availability. You’ll also see delivery windows and any promotions (e.g., first‑order discount).
3. **Order from a grocery chain** – If you’re near a Walmart or Target, you can often order a cake online for pickup or delivery through their own app or website.
4. **Try a specialty shop** – If you’re looking for something iconic (like a Magnolia Bakery cupcake tower), visit their website or call to confirm shipping options.

---

#### Need help finding a local spot?

If you tell me your city or zip code, I can suggest a handful of highly rated bakeries or delivery partners in your area. Just let me know!
